question: In many countries, people now wear Western clothes such as suits and jeans rather than traditional clothing. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?
essay_text:
The prevalence of Western-style clothes in the wardrobes of people is an increasingly noticeable trend in contemporary society in a lot of countries. This essay aims to explore the reasons behind this phenomenon and discuss its potential impacts.

There are two reasons for this tendency. One major reason is the globalized culture we live in today. Thanks to advanced technology and transportation, people can easily access information and products from other parts of the world, including fashion trends. As a consequence, western clothing styles have become more accessible and appealing to youngsters who seek diversity and individuality in their attire. Another factor that contributes to this tendency is the influence of media and popular culture. Celebrities, influencers, and movie characters often wear Western-style outfits, which set fashion trends and shape people’s perceptions of what is fashionable. As a result, many citizens emulate these styles, perceiving them as symbols of modernity and sophistication.

However, whether this trend is positive or negative depends on one’s perspective. On the positive side, it reflects cultural exchange and globalization, enabling citizens to appreciate different aesthetics and broaden their horizons. Moreover, it offers youngsters greater choices in expressing themselves through their clothing. On the other hand, some argue that excessive reliance on Western-style clothing could lead to a loss of traditional values and cultural identity. It might also contribute to consumerism, where individuals prioritize material possessions over deeper values like spirituality and interpersonal relationships.

In conclusion, the increasing preference for Western-style clothing among people results from globalization and media influences. While this trend has its advantages, it may also carry potential risks. Therefore, it is essential to maintain a balance between appreciating diverse cultures and preserving our own traditions.

The result is that more individuals are able to live in cities and enjoy higher standards of living, better healthcare, improved economic opportunity and various entertainment options. For the average resident, such development is incontestably positive.

However, new housing developments neglect the primacy of the natural world. Firstly, building homes on nearby farmland not only clears away pristine natural land but also necessitates the transportation of agricultural products from greater distances. This will in turn exacerbate environmental issues and potentially lead to inflated food costs for the average person. More importantly, cities that lack parks are not providing an optimal living environment for residents. For wealthy individuals, this is less pressing since they may be able to make frequent trips to outlying areas. Whereas, for the least privileged classes, parks may be their only opportunities to experience nature and a life deprived of all contact with the natural world is undeniably bleak.

In conclusion, despite the positives related to population density in cities, it is an overall negative due to its effect on the natural environment and quality of life in cities. Such proposals should therefore be pursued in moderation.

To conclude, I personally believe that green areas facilitate the healthy development of residents both mentally and physically. Therefore, governments should give favour to planting trees rather than building more houses.

essay_text:
The rise in popularity of online-learning software and applications has led many to argue they can be as effective as real-life lessons taken at university. In my opinion, though these lessons are more efficient in particular university situations, their overall efficacy is far lower than learning in person.

Proponents of online study point out how increased flexibility leads to greater efficiency. When students study in person, they must expend time traveling to and from class and waiting before and after the lesson. In the aggregate, this constitutes significant time lost. This time could be redirected into more studying or other tasks. For instance, a student studying online could finish assignments up until the minute class begins and quickly begin their homework after the lesson. However, the efficiency gained is largely hypothetical as most students are likely to become distracted during online lessons and waste much of the time saved online.

Moreover, in-person lessons are far more engaging than online ones. This was clearly evidenced during the recent Covid-19 pandemic when many schools, including universities, transitioned to online learning for a period of time. The results were that students were generally less engaged in lessons and their overall productivity and learning suffered. This counterintuitive loss of productivity can be explained not only by the potential distractions students are vulnerable to online but also by the lack of connection between learners and teachers. In a classroom setting, students personally interact with their professors and other students, guaranteeing a high level of engagement and memorability.

In conclusion, though there are reasons to argue for the potential time saved through online lessons, they are simply far less effective than real world classes. Online lessons should remain a niche element of a university education.

question: The best curriculum is not one based on a static body of knowledge, but one which teaches students to cope with change. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay_text:
In contemporary educational discourse, a prevailing viewpoint asserts that the most effective educational curriculum is not anchored in a static body of education but rather one that equips students with the skills to navigate and adapt to modification. This perspective emphasizes the dynamic nature of knowledge and the importance of cultivating a mindset that can thrive in an ever-evolving world. This essay aims to explore the merits and drawbacks of this ideology, examining its implications for both individual learners and the broader education system.

On one side of the argument, proponents of an educational curriculum centred on flexibility argue that in a rapidly changing global landscape, traditional static knowledge may quickly become outdated. The ability to cope with modification, problem-solve, and embrace new technologies becomes paramount for success in various fields. A curriculum that fosters resilience not only prepares students for the uncertainties of the future job market but also cultivates a mindset of continuous learning and resilience. Therefore, understanding the multifaceted implications of prioritizing flexibility over a fixed body of proficiency is crucial for evaluating its impact on the effectiveness of education.

Conversely, critics of this perspective contend that a curriculum devoid of a solid foundation in traditional proficiency may leave students without essential building blocks for critical thinking and decision-making. They argue that certain fundamental concepts and historical contexts provide a necessary framework for understanding the complexities of the modern world. Additionally, a focus on adaptability should not come at the expense of neglecting core principles and disciplines that have withstood the test of time. Striking a balance between resilience and a foundational knowledge base is essential to ensure that students possess both the resilience to navigate differences and the grounding to make informed choices.

In conclusion, while flexibility is crucial in the face of an ever-changing world, a balanced approach is necessary. An educational curriculum that combines a solid foundation of learning with the skills to cope with change is likely to be the most effective in preparing students for the challenges of the future. Therefore, the ideal educational curriculum is not one that rigidly adheres to a static body of learning or solely focuses on flexibility but rather one that synthesizes the strengths of both approaches, fostering a well-rounded and resilient generation of learners.

question: Instead of requiring primary school students to do experiments themselves, schools should only alllow them to watch experiments demonstrated by teachers. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Some educators feel that for students to learn effectively they must do experiments themselves, rather than simple observing their teachers. In my opinion, this sentiment has its limits, but in general pupils would benefit more from such a hands-on approach.

Detractors argue that it is more efficient to watch a teacher perform an experiment in front of the class. Throughout the course of the academic year, in classes such as chemistry, biology and physics, teachers will have to cover dozens of topics and highlight numerous theorems. The teacher may perform experiments in order to illustrate concepts when applicable. If students conduct these exercises instead, it would mean less time to go over other areas and would necessitate reducing the size of the curriculum. Their learning may achieve greater depth but the breadth would be abridged.

Nonetheless, performing an experiment oneself promotes greater understanding. Take for example a chemistry class. Students are only likely to remember the end result if the teacher explains the formula for a chemical reaction, selects the ingredients themselves and then mixes and highlights the process. In contrast, if the students must identify, measure and carefully follow steps on their own, they will commit this information more deeply to memory. Their later analysis will further reinforce a more complex understanding of the forces at play in a given experiment. Recent pedagogical research supports the contention that the physicality of performing is a powerful aid to memory and the key to long-term retention.

In conclusion, though there are legitimate reasons to not apply this rule without nuance, it is important that students generally be given the opportunity to carry out experiments on their own. What students internalize will be naturally more memorable.

Parenting has become a challenge these days as there is an increasing number of fathers who have become homemakers rather than acting as the customary breadwinner, which is now played by mothers. Financial difficulty is the foremost reason for this gender role reversals in rearing a family and in my opinion, this is a negative development.

The evident switch of parental figures is caused primarily by monetary issues a couple faces. Rearing of children tends to be expensive that either two parents need to work and hire help, which often requires more budget, or one stays at home. As more women are establishing their career with high position and pay, in gearing toward practicality, their husbands give way and sacrifice their own job to raise their offsprings at home. To be a good provider without neglecting childcare is the obvious reason for this modern approach in growing a household.

However, an issue about men's mental health could be a concern about this new approach of family structure. To be labelled as "househusband" could give detrimental effects as it is still a stigma in our society. These husbands could feel isolated as it will be uncomfortable for them to be in women-and-baby centres or have playdates with other kids. For instance, there are researches that found higher depressive symptoms with these stay-at-home dads. 

In conclusion, in my opinion, this change is prevalent now in order for these couples to tackle their finances with more ease without forfeiting the welfare of their children. Nonetheless, it should be applied with caution for the psychological ramifications it could present.

question: The increase in the production of consumer consumption goods results in damage to the natural environment. What are the causes of this and what can be done to solve this problem?
essay_text:
It is true that the production of consumer goods has increased significantly in recent years, leading to considerable damage to the natural environment. The primary reason for this issue is the influence of wasteful lifestyles, and the most effective solution is to raise public awareness about environmental protection.

On the one hand, there are two major causes of this problem. Firstly, the increasing demand for furniture has a detrimental impact on the environment. For instance, studies show that approximately 80% of individuals prefer furniture, such as tables and chairs, made from wood. As a result, excessive deforestation occurs to meet this demand, causing significant harm to forests and ecosystems. Secondly, the transportation of products contributes to air pollution. Automobiles and planes are widely used to deliver goods globally, and this reliance on fossil fuels releases harmful emissions into the atmosphere. Consequently, people may suffer from health problems such as respiratory diseases and even cancer due to polluted air.

On the other hand, governments can address this issue through two key measures. One effective solution is to promote environmental awareness by organizing educational programs and lectures that teach people how to protect their surroundings. For example, in the United Kingdom, citizens traditionally use wood to build homes; however, the government encourages the use of alternative materials like clay to preserve forests. This not only reduces environmental damage but also fosters sustainable practices. Additionally, authorities can encourage citizens to buy locally-produced goods instead of imported ones. This would support the national economy while reducing emissions caused by the transportation of foreign goods, leading to cleaner air and a healthier environment.

In conclusion, the production of consumer goods undoubtedly harms the environment, but this issue can be mitigated by increasing awareness and encouraging sustainable practices. Governments must take proactive steps to educate the public and promote environmentally friendly alternatives.

question: Some people say that now is the best time in history to be living. What is your opinion about this? What other time in history would be interesting ti live in?
essay_text:
Some argue that contemporary times represent the pinnacle of human existence, offering unparalleled opportunities, comfort, and knowledge. I largely concur with this perspective, although I also find certain historical epochs, such as the Renaissance or the Enlightenment, uniquely compelling. Ultimately, the assessment of the “best” era in which to live depends on whether one values material prosperity, personal freedom, or intellectual stimulation.

Undeniably, the modern era affords advantages that are unprecedented in human history. Advances in medicine and public health have drastically reduced mortality rates, eradicated or controlled many infectious diseases, and extended life expectancy to previously unimaginable levels. Coupled with these developments, the digital revolution has transformed access to information, education, and professional opportunities. In an instant, one can acquire knowledge that would have taken decades to obtain in the past, bridging geographical and cultural divides and fostering global interconnectedness. Such progress ensures that the present is arguably more conducive to personal and societal development than any previous epoch.

Furthermore, contemporary society generally provides a level of individual freedom and social mobility that historical populations could scarcely imagine. Gender equality, civil rights, and the rule of law have created environments in which people can pursue careers, beliefs, and lifestyles according to their aspirations, rather than being constrained by inherited status or social norms. In this respect, the present not only enhances quality of life materially but also cultivates intellectual and personal autonomy.

Nevertheless, it would be remiss to disregard the allure of previous eras. The Renaissance, for example, was a period of extraordinary cultural and intellectual flourishing. Living during this epoch would have allowed one to witness the genesis of revolutionary artistic, scientific, and philosophical ideas that laid the foundations of modern Western thought. Similarly, the Enlightenment championed rational inquiry, empirical evidence, and critical discourse, profoundly shaping political and philosophical paradigms. For individuals driven by curiosity, creativity, or the pursuit of knowledge, these historical periods might have offered experiences and intellectual stimulation unparalleled by the modern era.

In conclusion, while today arguably provides the optimal combination of technological, social, and personal advantages, certain historical periods retain a unique cultural and intellectual appeal. Ultimately, whether the present or the past constitutes the “best” era to live in is contingent upon one’s priorities: for material well-being, safety, and opportunity, contemporary life is unparalleled; for immersion in groundbreaking ideas and cultural renaissance, historical epochs such as the Renaissance or Enlightenment offer equally compelling alternatives.

question: It is better to learn the way people lived in the past through films and video records than written documents. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay_text:
n today's digital era, many argue that films and video records are more effective for learning about how people lived in the past compared to traditional written documents. While films undoubtedly offer vivid visualizations and immersive experiences, I believe both mediums have unique strengths in preserving history, and it is essential to strike a balance between them.

Films and video records bring historical events and lifestyles to life in ways that written documents often cannot. The ability to recreate settings, clothing, and mannerisms allows viewers to see and feel the past, fostering a deeper emotional connection. For example, historical films like Schindler’s List or 12 Years a Slave not only convey facts but also evoke empathy, helping audiences understand the human experiences behind historical events. Additionally, videos offer accessibility to a wide range of people, including those who may find reading difficult.

However, relying solely on films and videos can lead to a distorted or oversimplified understanding of the past. Filmmakers often dramatize or selectively present historical facts to enhance storytelling, which can result in inaccuracies. Written documents, on the other hand, provide a more detailed and reliable account of history. Texts such as diaries, letters, and official records offer primary sources that historians use to interpret the past with greater precision. They allow for nuanced analysis that may be lost in visual adaptations.

Moreover, written records offer a broader range of perspectives. While films focus on major historical events or prominent figures, written documents often capture the voices of ordinary people and reflect everyday life. They provide a window into different social classes, professions, and cultures, offering a more comprehensive understanding of how people lived in the past.

In conclusion, while films and videos are powerful tools for engaging with history, written documents remain invaluable for in-depth, accurate learning. A combination of both methods allows for a richer and more complete understanding of the past.

On the other hand, in recent years, science and technology have made tremendous strides. The new world demands work on innovative initiatives. Technological advancements provided vital support during this chaotic period, enabling online shopping and remote work. All these benefits are achievable through science and technology, making a strong case for their inclusion in the curriculum.

In summary, both arguments have their own merits and significantly contribute to our daily lives. I firmly believe that both views are equally valuable and beneficial. Therefore, both history and science and technology should be emphasized in today's curriculum.

question: Some believe that because everyone needs a place to live, governments should provide houses for those who are too poor to afford their own. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay_text:
There has been a controversy over whether governments should provide free or affordable housing for those who are homeless. In my opinion, while governments are responsible for assisting the homeless, I firmly believe that providing free or low-cost housing is not the most effective solution.

Housing is a fundamental human right, and the government should ensure that all citizens have access to safe living conditions. If the government takes responsibility for this, there would be multiple benefits. Firstly, providing accommodation can reduce crime rates. When individuals have stable housing, they are less likely to engage in criminal activities due to financial hardship. In this regard, the government should introduce policies that offer financial assistance to those who cannot afford housing. This would not only decrease homelessness but also help prevent the poverty cycle that often leads to criminal behaviour. Secondly, ensuring access to housing would allow people to allocate more resources towards physical activity, as their financial burdens would be lighter. Research has shown that when the government supports housing, such as providing financial assistance for homeownership, it increases participation in physical activities, which ultimately enhances productivity and public health.

However, despite the economic benefits of government housing assistance, there are significant downsides to this policy. If the government continues to invest heavily in free or low-cost housing, it could adversely affect the development of critical infrastructure. For example, in Taiwan, while the government’s housing support program has helped the poor, it has led to a reduction in funding for essential public services, such as sports facilities. In Taipei City, where the population is large, the lack of public sports centres has significantly limited access to physical exercise. A report showed that exercise participation has decreased by 20%, which in turn has reduced work efficiency and overall productivity. Therefore, many experts suggest that the government should prioritize investing in other sectors, such as healthcare, education, and infrastructure, in order to support long-term social development.

In conclusion, while it is essential for governments to assist the homeless, I strongly believe that providing free or low-cost housing is not the best approach. The government should instead focus on long-term solutions, such as investing in public sports facilities, healthcare, and education, which would help create a healthier and more self-sufficient society.

In conclusion, more self-reliant people are more likely to be successful and hold onto their homes. The role of government ought to be more subtle and include educational reforms aimed at opening up opportunities that individuals can themselves seize.

question: Some people think there should be a complete ban on all forms of advertising to what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay_text:
The issue of whether advertising should be completely banned is a topic of considerable debate. While some argue that all forms of advertising should be prohibited due to its manipulative nature and potential harm to consumers, I firmly disagree. In my opinion, advertising plays an essential role in both the economy and consumer choice, and a total ban would bring more harm than good.

Firstly, advertising serves as a vital tool for business growth and economic prosperity. In today’s highly competitive market, businesses rely on advertising to raise awareness of their products or services and differentiate themselves from competitors. Without advertising, many companies, particularly small businesses, would struggle to establish their presence, resulting in fewer job opportunities and a stagnant economy. For instance, global companies like Apple and Samsung depend on extensive advertising campaigns to promote their products worldwide. These ads not only help inform consumers about the latest technological innovations but also drive sales, which in turn stimulates the economy. Additionally, local businesses benefit from advertising by reaching potential customers within their communities. A complete ban on advertising would therefore create barriers to entry for new businesses and hinder the economic growth of existing ones.

Moreover, advertising plays a crucial role in providing consumers with valuable information. Consumers rely on advertisements to make informed choices about the products and services they purchase. Without ads, many individuals would be unaware of new or improved products that could enhance their lives. For example, healthcare ads inform the public about medications, wellness programs, and health services that can improve their quality of life. While some may argue that advertising often promotes unnecessary or harmful products, it is important to note that regulations are in place to ensure that advertisements are truthful and not misleading. Banning advertising entirely would deprive people of essential information that helps them make better purchasing decisions.

However, it is undeniable that there are some negative aspects of advertising that need to be addressed. For instance, advertisements can sometimes create unrealistic expectations or promote unhealthy lifestyles, particularly in the case of beauty or fast-food ads. While these issues should be taken seriously, the solution is not to ban advertising altogether but to enforce stricter regulations. Governments can impose guidelines that prevent misleading or harmful ads, particularly those targeting vulnerable groups such as children or those promoting addictive products like junk food or tobacco. In this way, the benefits of advertising can be maximized while minimizing its potential drawbacks.

In conclusion, while I acknowledge the concerns regarding the potential negative effects of advertising, I believe that a complete ban is not the solution. Advertising plays an indispensable role in business success, economic growth, and consumer awareness. Rather than eliminating it, governments should focus on enhancing regulatory frameworks to ensure that advertising remains ethical and transparent. A balanced approach, rather than an outright ban, would be the most effective way to address the issues while preserving the positive aspects of advertising.

There are only isolated cases when a shopper will see an ad and as a direct result make a purchase. For example, YouTube advertisements have included a feature to “skip ads” that has become an automatic response from nearly every viewer. Even when forced to watch ads, such as in the cinema before a film starts, consumers are unlikely to remember the products or services and there is a strong chance they will take out their phones to completely shut out distracting commercials.

Nonetheless, advertisements have a limited yet powerful efficacy . The strongest evidence for this comes from the enduring health of the advertising industry. This flourishing is because advertisements only need to yield results occasionally in order to be successful. For example, a fast food company such as McDonald’s or KFC might run an advertisement with the profitable expectation of only converting 1% of viewers, accepting the 99% failure rate as part of the business. Moreover, the 1% who make an immediate purchase is only one piece of the overall strategy. Advertising raises brand awareness and may lead to later consumption and even have a subliminal effect that is difficult to trace.

In conclusion, advertising is not designed to be effective at all times but instead to slowly influence and achieve the occasional success. In the aggregate, it is worthwhile for corporations to advertise even if the most common outcome is to be ignored.

Sending a man to the moon and maintaining expensive telescopes and space stations do nothing for the average person struggling to pay their bills and vulnerable to sudden economic downturns. Most may casually watch the moon landing or the occasional NASA video on YouTube but that is hardly justification for billions of dollars over decades that could have made a real difference if diverted towards medicine, education, infrastructure, and a vibrant employment sector.

Nonetheless, the effects pertain deeply to culture and science. Firstly, putting a man on the moon was a moment that transcends mundane utilitarian concerns. It not only was an exercise in the power and majesty of the human race but also inspired countless individuals across a wide variety of industries to push for great achievements and have pride in mankind. Secondly, the advances made while researching space have led to concrete, beneficial discoveries. For example, there are now satellites in space making possible phone calls and internet access nearly everywhere on Earth. Countless other large and small innovations from microchips to increased fuel efficiency are also to some degree indebted to the national funding of space exploration.

In conclusion, far from being a waste of valuable resources, space exploration has been the driving force behind the continued progress of humanity. It should therefore continue to receive support.

This essay will examine both perspectives before concluding with a reasoned standpoint.

Proponents of maximal information sharing argue that openness catalyzes progress across disciplines. In scientific research, for instance, open-access publications and data repositories enable peers to verify results, identify errors, and build upon existing work, thereby accelerating breakthroughs—especially in critical areas such as medical treatments and environmental science. Conversely, those who advocate for restricted information sharing underscore the necessity of protecting proprietary knowledge and sensitive data. In the corporate sphere, trade secrets, strategic plans, and patentable technologies constitute a company’s lifeblood; premature disclosure can erode competitive advantage, undermine profitability, and stifle research and development incentives. In scientific domains such as biotechnology or national defense, unregulated release of detailed methodologies or findings risks dual-use applications—where benign research may be co-opted for harmful purposes. Furthermore, academic researchers often invest years in generating novel insights; unrestricted sharing without adequate attribution could lead to plagiarism, misrepresentation, or unfair appropriation of intellectual credit.

In my view, an optimal approach balances the imperative for openness with the need for discretion. Establishing clear guidelines—such as tiered access levels, embargo periods for sensitive findings, and robust intellectual property frameworks—can ensure that information most beneficial to the public remains accessible, while confidential or potentially dangerous data are appropriately shielded. By coupling transparency with responsible stewardship, stakeholders can harness the virtues of information sharing without unduly compromising security or innovation incentives.

In conclusion, although free exchange of information underpins scientific advancement, educational equity, and economic collaboration, it must be tempered by safeguards that protect valuable or sensitive knowledge. Striking this equilibrium is essential to maximize societal benefits while mitigating potential risks.

Lastly, the sheer volume of shared information can lead to information overload, overwhelming individuals and impeding the absorption of truly valuable insights.

Striking a balance between the benefits and drawbacks of information sharing is essential. Policymakers and stakeholders must establish robust frameworks that safeguard intellectual property while encouraging the sharing of non-sensitive information. Trust mechanisms and authentication systems could be employed to ensure that information is shared responsibly and securely.

In conclusion, the question of how much information should be shared is not one-size-fits-all. The scientific and academic realms stand to gain immensely from an open exchange of ideas, which can lead to groundbreaking discoveries and advancements. However, in the business sector, particularly when it involves trade secrets, a more cautious approach is warranted. Ultimately, the goal should be to create an environment that fosters innovation and collaboration while safeguarding the rights and interests of individuals and organizations.

Thanks to that, Canada tops the 2019 ranking of countries in terms of happiness, equality, and citizens' security.

In conclusion, I fully agree that rules and laws are essential for a country's function and have to be strictly followed and obliged for every citizen of it. If a community did not have any rules or laws, it would lead to an appalling crime rate and violation of democratic rights and freedoms of people.

question: Some think that students must travel to another country in order to learn its language and customs. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Those with an academic interest in a given culture often do not need to travel there. This is particularly true if they are researching an historic period. For example, a scholar learning about Ancient Greece going there today, will only see ruins and a radically different culture. Ancient Greek is no longer even spoken. It would be much more profitable for a student of the Ancients to learn the language fluently on their own and become steeped in their histories and classic literature. The works of Euripides, Sophocles and Herodotus will provide far greater insight into the history, culture, and language of the Ancient Greeks than the few vestiges from thousands of years ago still standing today.

Nonetheless, cases like the one detailed above are rare and most people will benefit greatly from a more immersive experience. The difference between those studying abroad and learning in their own country is illustrative. Students attempting to learn English, for example, will need to be naturally adept at languages to become fluent without living in an English-speaking country. The majority of learners will improve faster when making daily transactions in English and learning in the real world outside the classroom. The cultural advantages are also self-evident. English movies and TV shows are realistic to varying degrees but pale in comparison to having actual foreign friends and experiencing firsthand their traditions and culture.

In conclusion, apart from esoteric academic study, nothing can replace the experience of living in another country. Anyone fully committed to understanding the culture and language of another country must factor in a period of time in residence there.

question: Some people believe that professionals, such as doctors and engineers, should be required to work in the country where they did their training. Others believe they should be free to work in another country if they wish. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
essay_text:
Some people believe that professionals such as doctors and engineers should be required to work in the home country where they completed their training. However, others argue that individuals should be free to work abroad. This essay will discuss both views before explaining why I believe professionals should have the freedom to work in another country for personal and professional growth. 

On the one hand, requiring professionals to work in their home country can help address the problem of brain drain. Many developing countries invest significant resources in educating doctors, engines, and other specialists. If these professionals leave immediately after graduation, the country may face a shortage of skilled workers. For example, hospitals and infrastructure projects rely heavily on trained experts to function effectively. Therefore, keeping these professionals in their home country can ensure that citizens receive adequate services and that national development continues. 

On the other hand, allowing professionals to work abroad provides important opportunities for personal and professional growth. In many developed countries, specialists can access advanced technology, better research facilities, and higher salaries. These experiences can help them develop new skills and gain international perspectives. In some cases, professionals may even return to their home country later with valuable knowledge that can benefit local industries and institutions. 

In conclusion, although requiring professionals to remain in their home country may help prevent skill shortages and support national development, individuals should ultimately have the freedom to work abroad. Gaining international experience can contribute to personal growth and may also benefit their home country if they return with valuable knowledge and expertise.

question: Some people believed that professionals, such as doctors and engineers, should be required to work in the country where they did their training. Others believe they shouuld be free to work in another country if they wish. Discuss both viewes and give your opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
essay_text:
Some people argue that doctors and engineers should be required to work in the country where they qualified, while others believe they should be free to take jobs abroad for higher pay, safer workplaces, or better training. I support mobility, because forced retention rarely fixes why people leave. Still, when training is heavily subsidised, a time-limited obligation is reasonable.

Supporters of compulsory local work focus on fairness and capacity. Professional training is expensive, and taxpayers often fund university places, teaching hospitals, and supervised placements. If graduates depart straight away, the public sector loses staff and its investment. This is felt most in remote areas: when a district hospital cannot replace a junior doctor, clinic lines stretch, referrals pile up, and emergency cover becomes fragile. Likewise, losing engineers slows infrastructure projects and weakens safety oversight on sites and in procurement.

However, strict restrictions can backfire. Many professionals migrate because the job is hard to do well: hospitals may lack equipment and safe staffing, while engineering roles may involve weak project governance, low pay, and limited mentoring. In field postings, morale drops quickly when targets stay high but resources do not, so compulsory placement feels like punishment rather than service. Bans also encourage avoidance, with some students choosing overseas study from the start. Mobility can raise skills too: doctors can train in better-equipped hospitals and return, while engineers bring back modern standards. Even those who stay overseas often support families through remittances and partnerships.

In conclusion, compulsory service may plug urgent gaps, but it cannot replace reform. Professionals should be free to work abroad, backed by fair two-to-four-year bonds or repayment options and better local conditions.

Some people argue that professionals such as doctors and engineers should be obliged to work in the country where they received their training, while others believe they should have the freedom to work abroad if they choose. This essay will discuss both views before presenting my own opinion.

On the one hand, requiring professionals to remain in the country where they were trained can bring significant benefits. In many cases, higher education—especially in fields like medicine and engineering—is heavily subsidized by governments. If graduates leave immediately after qualifying, the country that invested in their education may suffer a shortage of skilled workers and fail to see any return on its investment. This problem is particularly severe in developing nations, where the migration of doctors to wealthier countries can weaken healthcare systems and limit access to essential services for local populations. Therefore, mandatory service periods could help ensure that societies benefit from the professionals they helped to educate.

On the other hand, opponents of this view argue that professionals should not be restricted in their career choices. In an increasingly globalized world, freedom of movement is considered a fundamental right, and forcing individuals to work in a specific country may be unfair and demotivating. Moreover, allowing professionals to work abroad can have indirect benefits for their home countries. For example, they may send remittances, gain advanced skills and experience, or eventually return home with new knowledge and international networks. Such outcomes can contribute to long-term national development rather than harm it.

In my opinion, while governments are justified in wanting to protect their investment in education, completely restricting professionals’ mobility is neither practical nor ethical. A more balanced approach would be to encourage graduates to stay through incentives, such as competitive salaries or improved working conditions, or to require a limited period of service rather than a lifelong obligation.

In conclusion, although compelling arguments exist for requiring professionals to work in their training country, I believe that individuals should ultimately have the freedom to choose where they work, provided that fair and flexible policies are in place to support national interests.

question: Some people believe that professionals, such as doctors and engineers, should be required to work in the country where they did their training. Others believe they should be free to work in another country if they wish. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Some people argue that professionals trained within a country, such as doctors and engineers, should be obliged to serve that country after completing their education. Others, however, believe that these individuals should have full freedom to work abroad. While mandatory service may help reduce skill shortages, I believe professionals should be free to choose where they work, as mobility encourages fairness, personal development and global progress.

On the one hand, requiring highly skilled workers to work in the country where they were trained can bring several benefits. First, many nations—especially developing ones—often invest substantial public resources in subsidising medical and engineering education. In such cases, compulsory service ensures that society receives a return on its investment. Second, retaining trained professionals can help address critical shortages in essential sectors. For example, in rural areas, a lack of doctors and engineers can hinder economic development and public health, and a mandatory service period could alleviate this problem by guaranteeing a stable workforce.

On the other hand, allowing professionals to decide freely where to work is crucial for individual rights and overall global advancement. Skilled workers may seek better working conditions, more advanced facilities or higher salaries abroad, which are necessary for their personal and career development. Restricting their movement could be seen as limiting their freedom and discouraging ambition. Moreover, when professionals are allowed to work internationally, the global exchange of knowledge becomes possible. Doctors and engineers who gain experience overseas often bring back new techniques, technologies and management practices, which ultimately benefit their home countries in the long run.

In my view, although requiring service within the training country may temporarily ease labour shortages, it is neither sustainable nor fair in the long term. Governments should instead create attractive working environments—such as competitive salaries, good career prospects and safe conditions—to encourage professionals to stay voluntarily. Freedom of movement, combined with supportive national policies, is a far more effective way to retain talent and promote development.

In conclusion, both mandatory service and free movement have their merits, but ensuring freedom of choice while improving domestic conditions offers the most balanced and beneficial approach.

question: In the past, most people worked for small businesses, while more people now work for large businesses. What are the advantages and disadvantages of working for large businesses?
essay_text:
In recent times, there has been a noticeable shift from employment in small enterprises to positions in more substantial corporations. Such a move has reshaped the employment landscape and has brought with it both benefits and drawbacks. This essay will focus on two primary advantages of working for large businesses: stability and job security, and opportunities for career advancement. Conversely, we will also examine two pronounced disadvantages: the pervasive feeling of anonymity and the challenges posed by bureaucracy.

One of the most appealing facets of working for a large business is the stability and job security it offers. Big corporations often have a robust financial footing, enabling them to navigate economic downturns with fewer layoffs or salary cuts. This stability can provide employees with peace of mind, knowing that their livelihoods are relatively secure. Such security is invaluable, especially in uncertain economic times, and can greatly influence job satisfaction and loyalty.

Furthermore, large businesses often come with a hierarchy that presents multiple tiers of management and specialization. This structure inherently provides opportunities for career advancement. Employees in such environments have a clearer pathway to climb the corporate ladder, access higher salaries, and attain more prestigious positions. The allure of growth and progression is a significant pull factor attracting talents to large corporations.

However, with these benefits come certain challenges. A common sentiment echoed by employees in vast enterprises is the feeling of anonymity. In such expansive work environments, individuals can often feel like mere cogs in a machine, devoid of identity or significance. This sense of detachment can lead to reduced motivation, a lack of personal investment in the company's mission, and even feelings of alienation.

Another significant drawback of large corporations is their propensity for bureaucracy. Decision-making processes can be painstakingly slow, with approvals required from multiple levels of management. This hierarchical approach can stifle innovation, as employees might be deterred from suggesting improvements or new ideas, fearing they will get entangled in red tape. Furthermore, the day-to-day operations can become cumbersome, leading to inefficiencies and frustration among staff.

In conclusion, while the allure of stability and upward mobility makes large businesses attractive to many, it's essential to weigh these benefits against the potential downsides. The impersonal nature of vast corporations and the challenges posed by bureaucracy can sometimes overshadow the positives. As the employment landscape continues to evolve, it remains crucial for individuals to carefully assess both sides of the coin before making career decisions.

Moreover, the expenses are also more than the small businesses as it has to operate more production activities.

To conclude, entrepreneurs should be more careful before they start moving on to large businesses, because, to operate larger companies they must acquire adequate knowledge to deal with the adverse side.

question: In the past, most people worked for small businesses, while more people now work for large businesses. What are the advantages and disadvantages of working for large businesses?
essay_text:
The rise of large corporations has led to a fundamental shift in the workforce towards large businesses. The chief advantages of this relate to opportunity and the downsides are larger, societal dilemmas.

Proponents of big business can point to career advancement and the variety of roles within a large company. Small businesses, by their nature, draw on a limited possible source of revenue that naturally caps promotions. Large companies have nearly unlimited profit potential and can thus employ a large number of managers, executives and other high-salaried positions. Moreover, a small business is more likely to be limited in the number of roles, while larger companies will have departments ranging from legal to marketing to research and development to human resources, all of which are potential destinations for motivated employees.

The disadvantages of these large companies relate less directly to individuals and more to society at large. Firstly, although there are more quality jobs available in big companies, the disappearance of small, local entrepreneurs means that capital becomes concentrated in the company’s chief shareholders, who are often living in other countries and already extremely rich. Over time this has led to the division of wealth that defines the 21st century. Secondly, as executive decisions become further removed from local communities it is harder to regulate large companies. A good example of this would be the environmental cost of drilling for oil and extracting natural gas, which hurts local residents but continues unabated because those in authority are unaffected.

In conclusion, the opportunities provided by big business do not outweigh the negative potential for all of society when power becomes concentrated and distant. It is therefore important to check the reach of corporations and empower individuals.

question: In the past, most people worked for small businesses, while more people now work for large businesses. What are the advantages and disadvantages of working for large businesses?
essay_text:
Present-day workers often opt to pursue careers with well-known businesses as opposed to working for small-time businesses such as in the past. Big enterprises offer job security, although life in the workplace tends to be more stressful.

The advantages often relate to professional stability. Large businesses rely heavily on the number of their front-liners and without them, their business will suffer, thereby lessening the maximum potential income they can get. Due to this, employees do not need to worry about losing their jobs. At the same time, career advancement is almost always a possibility when working for large companies. The more employees a company has, the more managers will be needed to supervise the overall operation of the businesses and this opens up doors for workers who want to advance their careers. A report from Oxford University in March 2020 revealed that established businesses in the UK have 38% managerial roles as compared to 15%, from start-up companies.

Contrarily, stress is the primary disadvantage of working for such companies. Firstly, due to the demands of their responsibilities, employees are often forced to work within strict schedules and because of this, they often do not get enough chances to spend time on holidays or family vacations. Secondly, to keep up with the growing demands from their consumers, big businesses often have demanding managers who constantly drive their employees beyond their limitations. Their high expectations take a toll on the mental and physical health of the workers, which have long-term negative repercussions on their overall well-being.

In conclusion, job stability and career growth are extremely attractive to modern-day workers, although they would need to determine first if they can put up with the high level of pressure in the workplace. Whether it is a trade-off that they are willing to take, is a question only they can answer.

Certain individuals will always demand employment security. First, reality is inevitable, and steady job is required to meet our daily needs. Additionally, a continuous stay in a company makes it easier to receive a promotion. For those who place a premium on job fulfilment, however, satisfaction, accomplishments, and the quest of life's meaning are of paramount importance. Those independent artists who live an unpredictable lifestyle, for example, strive for their dreams rather than the steady income. In addition, employees who are satisfied with their jobs tend to be self-motivated and dedicated to their careers.

Nevertheless, sustaining job satisfaction does not imply sacrificing job security, or vice versa. In fact, contentment and sustainability criteria can vary from person to person. For instance, some individuals find satisfaction in educating others; therefore, being a teacher, a very stable vocation, allows them to realise their both goals at the same time.

In conclusion, my viewpoint is that job satisfaction and job security are equally important, and that it is possible to strike a compromise between the two when seeking employment.

question: Some people think that governments should support retired people financially while others believe they should take care of themselves. Discuss both views and give you own opinion.
essay_text:
Many individuals believe that people should be self-sufficient in managing their financial needs after retirement, while others argue that the government ought to provide support to retirees. Although it can be argued that the state has a duty to give back to society by offering assistance to the elderly, I believe that encouraging individuals to take responsibility for their own financial security fosters discipline and long-term sustainability.

On the one hand, governments do carry a responsibility toward their citizens. Many individuals spend decades working and contributing taxes that sustain national infrastructure and public services. It may therefore seem reasonable that the state provides financial assistance once these individuals retire. In several developed nations, such as the UK, state pensions are designed to ensure that elderly citizens are not left in financial hardship. Such measures can reduce poverty among retirees and guarantee a basic standard of living. However, excessive reliance on government support may discourage personal savings and place considerable fiscal strain on public finances, particularly in ageing societies.

On the other hand, individuals who plan for their own retirement are more likely to develop financial discipline. When people understand that their future security depends largely on their own savings, they are motivated to adopt responsible spending habits during their working years. For example, employees in India contribute to the Provident Fund, where a portion of their salary is set aside to support them after retirement. Since this fund is built from their own earnings, it promotes financial awareness and self-reliance rather than dependency. Over time, such systems can create a more economically stable and independent population.

In conclusion, while governments should ensure that elderly citizens do not fall into poverty, I believe that individuals should primarily take responsibility for their retirement savings. Encouraging financial independence not only reduces pressure on public resources but also cultivates a culture of discipline and foresight.
